Esarhaddon
ee-sar-HAD-un
n. (proper, a king of Assyria; Assyrian, Ashur has given a brother)
Assyrian Ashur-aha-iddina, Ashur has given a brother. Son of Sennacherib, he came to the throne over his father's murdered body, and the Authorized Version names him three times — twice in the same sentence recorded in two books, and once in the mouth of Judah's enemies.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah had prophesied that Sennacherib would return to his own land and fall by the sword there, and the fulfilment is recorded twice in identical words: “And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead” (2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38). The king who had mocked the God of Israel died at the feet of an idol that could not defend him, killed by his own sons, and Esarhaddon inherited the throne. His name surfaces again a century and a half later, when the adversaries of Judah offer to help rebuild the temple: “we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither” (Ezra 4:2). The mixed population he had settled in Samaria had a mixed religion, and Zerubbabel refused the offer.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; the sense is fixed by Scripture, where Esarhaddon is the son of Sennacherib who reigned in his stead after his murder.

expand to see more

ASSYRIA, n. An ancient kingdom of western Asia, whose capital was Nineveh, long the scourge and at last the captor of the northern kingdom of Israel.

IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.

USURP, v.t. To seize and hold in possession by force or without right; as, to usurp a throne.

SAMARITAN, n. An inhabitant of Samaria; one of a people formed from the mingling of foreign colonists with the remnant of Israel.

SYNCRETISM, n. The attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance with each other.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 19:37 — "And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead."

Isaiah 37:38 — "And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Armenia: and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead."

Ezra 4:2 — "Then they came to Zerubbabel, and to the chief of the fathers, and said unto them, Let us build with you: for we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither."

Ezra 4:3 — "But Zerubbabel, and Jeshua, and the rest of the chief of the fathers of Israel, said unto them, Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God; but we ourselves together will build unto the LORD God of Israel, as king Cyrus the king of Persia hath commanded us."

Modern Corruption

Offers of religious partnership from those who sacrifice to the LORD alongside other gods are welcomed today as generous ecumenism; Zerubbabel refused exactly such an offer from the people Esarhaddon had settled.

expand to see more

Ezra 4 records one of the most instructive refusals in Scripture, and it is regularly judged narrow. The adversaries approach with warm words: Let us build with you: for we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither. Everything about it sounds cooperative. 2 Kings 17 tells the reader what their religion actually was — they feared the LORD and served their own gods — and Zerubbabel answered that they had nothing to do with the house of God, but that Israel alone would build. A shared vocabulary about God is not a shared faith, and the test of partnership is the doctrine, not the warmth of the offer.

The other half of Esarhaddon's appearance is a lesson in how God answers blasphemy. Sennacherib had sent letters asking whether the God of Jerusalem could deliver better than the gods of Hamath and Arpad. Isaiah answered that he would return by the way he came and not shoot an arrow into the city, and he did. The end came not in battle but in a temple: the great king worshipping Nisroch, and his own sons behind him with swords. The God who is mocked does not always answer at once, and when he answers he frequently uses the mocker's own household.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Assyrian Ashur-aha-iddina, Ashur has given a brother; Hebrew Ecarchaddown (H634); Cancheriyb (H5576), Sennacherib; Nicrok (H5268), Nisroch.

expand to see more

Hebrew Ecarchaddown (H634) — Esarhaddon; the Assyrian Ashur-aha-iddina, Ashur has given a brother.

Hebrew Cancheriyb (H5576) — Sennacherib, his father, slain while worshipping.

Hebrew Nicrok (H5268) — Nisroch, the god in whose house Sennacherib died.

Hebrew Ashshuwr (H804) — Asshur, Assyria; the rod of God's anger in Isaiah 10.

Hebrew Shomrown (H8111) — Samaria; where Esarhaddon's colonists were planted.

Usage

"“And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead” — after a murder in a temple."

"“Since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur” — the offer Zerubbabel refused."

"“Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God”."
